children.text: A former US military rest camp set in the pine forest southeast of downtown Baguio. Walk the historical core with the Bell Amphitheater, the Bell House and the "Cemetery of Negativism," then enjoy a forest picnic or a round of golf — the most peaceful half day you can spend in Baguio.
Camp John Hay is a former US military rest camp set in a pine forest about
above sea level,
10–15 minutes
by car from Session Road in downtown Baguio. The US 48th Infantry set up a "Hill Station" here in
, and on
October 25, 1903

an executive order by President Theodore Roosevelt made it a military reservation. It was named after John Hay, the US Secretary of State at the time. Much cooler than the lowlands, it served as a highland retreat where American soldiers and their families came to rest.
In World War II, Japanese bombers struck the camp on the morning of
December 8, 1941
, making it the first place in the Philippines to be bombed. During the occupation it served as a civilian internment camp and as the headquarters of General Tomoyuki Yamashita, and on
September 3, 1945

Yamashita surrendered at the former High Commissioner's residence. That residence is now the summer residence of the US ambassador and is not open to the public. After the war the camp became John Hay Air Base in
, and it was returned to the Philippine government on
July 1, 1991
After the handover, a private developer took a long-term lease in
and built hotels, a golf course and shops, but after a long dispute a Supreme Court ruling let the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) take back the facilities in
January 2025

. Today the state-owned John Hay Management Corporation (JHMC) manages the estate, and the former Manor and Forest Lodge operate under the name "John Hay Hotels." Visitors have kept coming since the change in management — about 4.15 million in the first half of
alone — and in
April 2026
a new meditation garden, Tranquility Park, opened.

The estate spreads out over a historical core with the Bell Amphitheater, the Bell House and the "Cemetery of Negativism," picnic grounds and forest paths under the pines, a golf course designed by Jack Nicklaus, and hotels and restaurants. It suits travelers who want to escape the crowds and fumes of downtown for half a day in a cool forest, families looking for a picnic with children, and anyone who wants to trace the American colonial era and the war on foot.

The heart of the historical core, where terraced flower beds cut into a pine-covered slope ring a green-roofed gazebo. It is said to have been designed by General J. Franklin Bell, then commander in the Philippines, and today it is a photo spot that hosts weddings and outdoor events.
An American-style wooden house built around

that served as a summer home for US Army commanders. Today it is a small museum displaying period furniture and old photographs, and its wide veranda looks out over the pine forest. Entry is with the historical core ticket (
for adults).
Not a real graveyard but a hillside lined with playful tombstones that invite you to "bury" bad habits such as laziness and procrastination. It is said to have been created in the
early 1980s
by a commander of John Hay Air Station, and reading the epitaphs one by one is half the fun.

Along the forest path that runs beside the Bell House steps, signboards tell the camp's story from the Hill Station days to Yamashita's surrender. At the end of the path, the Secret Garden is a quiet nook surrounded by tall pines.

blocks.title: Liberty Loop and the totem pole

children.text: A replica of the Statue of Liberty, a symbol of the American era, stands at the end of a walking path. On a wooden totem pole nearby, the faces of figures tied to the history of the camp and Baguio — John Hay, Theodore Roosevelt, Douglas MacArthur and others — are carved one above another.

Spread out a packed lunch at the picnic grounds, where green tables are scattered under the Benguet pines. Early in the morning, fog settles over the forest for a special atmosphere, and there are wide lawns for children to run around.
An 18-hole, par-69 course designed by Jack Nicklaus, with bentgrass greens that are rare in the Philippines. Public green fees announced at the reopening in
January 2025
were
on weekdays and
on weekends, with carts and caddies paid separately.
A meditation garden of about 896㎡ that opened in
April 2026
. Symmetrical walkways and rest areas surround a central meditation statue, making it a good place to catch your breath after touring the historical core.

Buy the historical core ticket and walk down through the terraced flower beds of the Bell Amphitheater
See the old furniture and photos inside the Bell House and look out over the forest from the veranda
Follow the History Trail and take a short rest in the Secret Garden
Visit the Cemetery of Negativism, then the Liberty Loop and the totem pole
Have lunch at a John Hay Hotels restaurant or another eatery on the estate, then head back downtown
Breathe the morning air on a walk through the foggy picnic grounds and forest paths

2–3 hours
touring the historical core (Bell Amphitheater, Bell House, History Trail, Cemetery of Negativism)

. If you are coming from abroad, fly into Clark International Airport (CRK) and take the Genesis (Joybus) direct bus to Baguio, about

From downtown spots such as Session Road and Burnham Park, a taxi takes
10–15 minutes
and costs about
. Tell the driver "Camp John Hay Historical Core" or "Bell House" and you will be dropped off in front of the historical core.
The estate is large and hilly, so a taxi can be hard to find on the way back. Use the pickup points in front of the hotels or along the main road.
From downtown, jeepneys bound for John Hay, such as those marked "Scout Barrio," drop you on the main road inside the estate. The minimum fare for traditional jeepneys has been
since
September 28, 2026
, and fares run about
depending on distance.
Routes and stops change often, so tell the driver where you want to get off when you board.
The drive from Manila takes about
4–6 hours
via NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX and then up Marcos Highway to Baguio. Kennon Road is often closed for rockfall and repairs, so check whether it is open before you set off.
Parking on the estate is free or paid depending on the facility. On weekends the spaces around the historical core fill up early, so it is best to arrive in the morning.
The free electric shuttle that ran in
was suspended for a safety review after an accident on
January 16, 2026
. Check on site whether it is running again; if not, walk or take a taxi.
1–2 hours
on foot is enough for the historical core, but there are many steps and slopes, so wear comfortable shoes.
Camp John Hay is mostly outdoors, so the weather makes or breaks a visit. Baguio's average annual temperature is about
, and the dry season from
November–April
is clear and cool — the best time for walking the forest paths. Early mornings in
December–February
drop to around
, bringing fog to the pine forest. In
February
all of Baguio is packed for the Panagbenga Flower Festival, which in
ran from
February 1
to
March 8
March–May
is the warm-day peak season, busiest during Holy Week and the summer school break. In the rainy season from
June–October

, afternoon showers and thick fog are common and passing typhoons bring heavy rain, so forest paths can be slippery and picnics difficult. In the rainy season, finish your plans in the morning and bring a raincoat. Festival dates change every year, so check the latest announcements.

To stay on the estate, the main options are John Hay Hotels' Garden Wing, the former Manor, and the Forest Wing, the former Forest Lodge. The two buildings are connected so guests share the facilities, and rates run about
a night depending on room and season. They are ideal for quiet nights in the forest and early-morning walks; to save money, stay at a guesthouse around Session Road or Burnham Park (about
a night) and come by taxi. Book early for Panagbenga and Holy Week.

The Garden Wing's restaurant, Le Chef, serves breakfast buffets and Western dishes with garden views, while the Forest Wing's The Twist serves Asian cuisine. For a picnic, pick up Baguio's signature strawberry and ube jams, bread and fruit at a downtown market or bakery. Restaurants and cafés in the estate's commercial area are still being reorganized after the change in management, so check that the place you want is open before you go.
The historical core is generally open
. Go in right after opening, before tour groups arrive, to photograph the amphitheater at leisure.
One historical core ticket covers the Bell House, the Bell Amphitheater and the Cemetery of Negativism. Bring ID if you want the student, senior or PWD discount.
Tickets and taxis are often paid in cash, so carry plenty of small bills such as
and
There are many steps and dirt paths, so wear non-slip sneakers and bring a raincoat in the rainy season.
Even at midday the shade is cool, and mornings and evenings are chilly. Bring a light jacket.
Take your picnic trash home or put it in the designated bins. The management asks visitors to follow "Clean As You Go" (CLAYGO).
The management sometimes opens the historical core for free on anniversaries or holidays. Check the John Hay Management Corporation (JHMC) announcements before your visit.
On weekend mornings (
), solo and twosome golf flights may be restricted, so book ahead and make up your group.
Since the change in management in
January 2025
, hotel names, fees, the shuttle and shop operations have kept changing. Don't rely only on old blog posts — check the latest announcements.
Tree Top Adventure, once known for its ziplines, is reported to have closed. Don't go there based on old reviews.
The forest eco-trails have been closed several times because of damage and inspections of unauthorized alterations. If the trailhead is blocked off, do not enter.
Cars move fast on the estate's roads and some sidewalks are narrow. In
January 2026
a shuttle accident on the estate killed a pedestrian, so keep a firm hold of children's hands.
After rain, steps and forest paths are slippery with moss and pine needles. Avoid unlit forest paths after dark.
Some buildings and areas, including the US ambassador's residence, are off-limits. Follow the fences and the guards' instructions.
